## Exercise 8.1

Zellner's $g$ prior [@Zellner:1986] for linear regression takes the form 
\begin{align*}
\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \sigma^2, \mathbf{X} &\sim \mathsf{Gauss}_p\left(\boldsymbol{\beta}_0, \frac{n}{\kappa_0}\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\right)\\
p(\sigma^2) &\propto \frac{1}{\sigma^2}
\end{align*}
which gives a prior variance proportional to that of the sampling distribution of the ordinary least squares estimator, which is $$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sim \mathsf{Gauss}_p\{\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\}.$$
Note that the prior is conditional on the covariates, which are assumed to be exogeneous.


a) Show that Zellner's $g$ prior gives rise to a conjugate prior and derive the posterior mean and covariance.


:::{.solution}

This follows the same derivation as the Gaussian - inverse gamma model in the chapter on regression models.

The data distribution is 
\begin{align*}
\boldsymbol{Y} \mid \boldsymbol{\beta}, \mathbf{X}, \sigma^2 &\sim \mathsf{Gauss}_n(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2\mathbf{I}_n)\\
\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \mathbf{X}, \sigma^2 & \sim \mathsf{Gauss}_p\left\{ \boldsymbol{\beta}_0, \frac{n}{\kappa_0}\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\right\} \\
p(\sigma^2) &\propto \sigma^{-2}.
\end{align*}
The log posterior is
\begin{align*}
\log p(\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2 \mid \boldsymbol{y}, \mathbf{X}) &\propto -\frac{n}{2} \log(\sigma^2) -\frac{(\boldsymbol{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^\top (\boldsymbol{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})}{2\sigma^2} -  \frac{1}{2}\log \det\left( \frac{\kappa_0}{n\sigma^2}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\right) \\&- \frac{\kappa_0(\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_0)^\top \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} (\boldsymbol{\beta}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_0)}{2n\sigma^2} 
\end{align*}
and note that, by properties of determinants,
\begin{align*}
\log \det\left( \frac{\kappa_0}{n\sigma^2}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\right)
&= \log\left\{\left(\frac{\kappa_0}{n\sigma^2}\right)^{p}\det\left( \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\right)\right\}
\\&\stackrel{\sigma^2}{\propto} -p  \log(\sigma^2).
\end{align*}
Thus, if we expand the quadratic forms and take $c^{-1}=1+\kappa_0/n,$ we find that the log posterior for $(\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2)$ is proportional to
\begin{align*}
\log p(\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2 \mid \boldsymbol{y}, \mathbf{X}) &\propto -(n+p+1)\log(\sigma^2) \\&\qquad - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\left(\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} - 2\boldsymbol{y}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{y}^\top\boldsymbol{y}\right) \\&\qquad - \frac{\kappa_0}{2n\sigma^2}\left(\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}-2\boldsymbol{\beta}_0^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\beta}_0\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_0\right)
 \\&=-(n+p+1)\log(\sigma^2) \\&\qquad -\frac{1}{2c\sigma^2}\left(\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} - 2\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right) \\
& \qquad  + \frac{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}/c - \boldsymbol{y}^\top\boldsymbol{y} - (\kappa_0/n)\boldsymbol{\beta}_0\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_0}{2\sigma^2}
\end{align*}
and, upon writing $\boldsymbol{y}^\top\mathbf{X} = \boldsymbol{y}^\top\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}),$ we get that 
\begin{align*}
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} &= c\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} + (1-c)\boldsymbol{\beta}_0
\end{align*}
We see that this is the joint distribution $p(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \sigma^2, \boldsymbol{y}, \mathbf{X}) p(\sigma^2 \mid \boldsymbol{y}, \mathbf{X})$, where
\begin{align*}
\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid \sigma^2, \boldsymbol{y}, \mathbf{X} & \sim \mathsf{Gauss}_{p}\left\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, c\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\right\} \\
\sigma^2 \mid  \boldsymbol{y}, \mathbf{X} & \sim \mathsf{inv. gamma}\left(n + p, \frac{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}{2c} - \frac{\boldsymbol{y}^\top\boldsymbol{y}}{2} - \frac{\kappa_0\boldsymbol{\beta}_0\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_0}{2n}\right).
\end{align*}
This is a conjugate model, since the (improper) prior can be viewed as a limiting member of the inverse gamma distribution when the scale parameter $b \to 0.$ As usual, the prior mean is a weighted average of the maximum likelihood estimator (here the ordinary least square estimator) and the prior mean.

:::

b) What is the benefit of this relative to an isotropic prior covariance $\sigma^2\mathbf{I}_p$ for $\beta \mid \sigma^2$?

:::{.solution}

The model is now invariant to linear change of units. Indeed, consider the case with a single covariate $\mathbf{x}^{\star}_1 \mapsto 2\mathbf{x}_1.$ Then, the corresponding coefficient $\beta_1$ shrinks, and the posterior would have $\widehat{\beta}_1^{\star} = \widehat{\beta}_1/2$. The $g$-prior directly incorporates the change through the variance term $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}.$

:::

c) Give an interpretation to $\kappa_0$: what happens when $\kappa_0=1$? or $\kappa_0=n$?

:::{.solution}

We can establish that the posterior mean is a weighted average of the maximum likelihood $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},$ the OLS estimator, and the prior mean $\boldsymbol{\beta}_0.$ If $\kappa_0=1,$ then the prior weight for the prior is $1/n,$ corresponding to a phantom observation for a sample of size $n+1.$ By contrast, taking $\kappa_0=n$ gives prior weight $1/2$ regardless of the sample size, which is clearly undesirable as the prior does not vanishes. 

:::
